title: Canto Six. Sannyasa
html:
The students' insults and the resolve to take sannyasa; talks with Shachi and Vishnupriya; departure at night; sannyasa from Keshava Bharati at Katwa; three days in Radha-desha; the cowherd boys' trick; Advaita at the Ganga: "This is Vrindavana"; Shantipura; the feast at Advaita's house and the jests with Nityananda; the arrival of Shachi and the devotees (pp. 28–32)

[p. 28]

1Once the Lord, abused without any cause in the town by students wandering here and there with harsh words, thought thus:

2"If they perish by reviling Me — alas, what use is My mercy? Wishing to show mercy to these townspeople, even to those whose speech is harsh, I shall take sannyasa.

3For those on earth who offend Me there is no other way: their way is to bow to Me; and [to bow] to a sannyasi is easy even for offenders."1

4Having thought this over, the Lord went home and at nightfall said to His mother in private: "Mother, how does this world appear to you? What do you perceive in your heart?

5To Me it seems like death itself, terrible. Therefore, having restrained oneself and pacified [the senses], fixing the heart on this, one must conquer it — worshipping the feet of Hari, one must be freed."

6When the Lord finished, Shachi, turning pale, seeing Him as if already walking the path of those who wear garments of bark, said nothing to her son, detached from everything.2

7Having said this, Gaurahari, again and again soothing her sorrow, spent some days at home, sporting with His pure wife.

8The beloved served her husband seeing Him as Hari, her in-laws and friends seeing them as elders; with good understanding, as a chaste wife, she enjoyed for a short time [the company of] the Lord, seeing Him as God.

9One night the moon among knowers of mantras said to His unsuspecting wife: "Listen, O you who walk like a she-elephant: you have been kindled by the Creator of the world for the world, like a lamp.3

10Seeing constantly your tender body, shining only briefly like the unstable form of lightning, I am grieved today in the depths of My heart.

11The Lord who is victorious in the world suddenly parts a pair of lovers; know that this is always His play; we should not grieve over it.

12Therefore it has long seemed right to Me to remain unchanged even when a benefactor perishes; and you, do not pine in vain in separation from your kin.

13He is dear to all embodied beings for whose sake all things are dear; therefore place your mind in the form of Hari and find peace in the Enchanting One."4

14Having spoken these words, the Lord, who knows the meaning, embraced His wife and fell silent; but she, though embraced, found no joy, remembering the words of the Lord.

15With flowers, ornaments, perfumes, new clothes, jests and loving play He pleased the woman and, content, again took delight with her through the night.

16And at dawn, when a breeze blew from the slightly opening lotuses, the Lord, knowing no fear, leaving her asleep like a [set-aside] leaf-cup of offering remnants (nirmalya), went out of the house.5

[p. 29]

17This young couple, like a pair of chakravakas by day, having taken much delight through the night — alas! — fell into the calamity of a separation of the night: the will of the Creator is never otherwise.6

18Learning of the Lord's intention, Mukunda, Acharya-mani [Chandrashekhara], the best of the twice-born, and the avadhuta, leaving behind worldly happiness, gladly followed Him.

19The Lord, knowing that the righteous would follow Him, fearing obstacles, resolved to take sannyasa and set out in haste the next day for the town named Katuka [Katwa].

20There the Lord came to Keshava Bharati and, bowing, [asked] for sannyasa; at his command, His lovely curls shorn, He became a mendicant monk who kept the shikha and the sacred thread.7

21When the twenty-fourth year had passed, in the bright fortnight of the month of Tapas, on Hari's day, having received Vaishnava initiation on earth, the Lord, intoxicated with the nectar of the Name, bowed down [to the guru].

22Adorned with staff, kaupina and waterpot, the Wise One, having taken leave of the guru too, resolving to go Himself to His own abode, Gokula, set out, free of the taint of desire.

23Not distinguishing His own body, the directions or places, drenched in the wine of joy and love, the king of sannyasis wandered hither and thither for three days in the land of Radha.8

24On the next day at sunrise three, headed by the avadhuta, saw the Lord. He asked them: "Why have you come here?" They replied: "To go with You to Vraja."

25Going with them, He asked some cowherd boys to show Him the way to Vrindavana; and they, instructed by the avadhuta, pointed out the way to the Ganga: "This is the road to Vraja."

26When in the morning the Lord, deceived by the boys' words, went toward the river of the gods, the incarnation of Balarama, having quickly thought it through, [said] secretly to Acharya-mani:

27"Go on ahead and tell Advaita everything the Lord is doing — in His name. Then quickly go on to Navadvipa, bring Shachi and show her her son."

28Thus instructed, the best of brahmins went to the Acharya and told him everything, and then, composed, to soothe Shachi's grief, went on from there to Navadvipa.

29The Lord, impelled by the false words of the sons of Vraja, rapt in prema, on the next day came to the best of rivers, the Vishnupadi, and with a jubilant heart threw Himself into it.

30"Ah, He Himself has fallen into the water that flows from His own big toe, and is Himself drowning in it!" — saying this, the two companions, holding His lotus hands, laughed.9

31Then Advaita, having crossed that river by boat, joyfully came up to Him and said: "Lord, put on this dry [cloth] and leave the wet kaupina here."

32Hearing his gentle words, Gaura, covering His body with embarrassment, said: "We have come to Vrindavana; how is it that you are here? You amaze us."

[p. 30]

33To this the humble best of brahmins, standing on the bank, smiling, said to Him: "Vrindavana is the abode where You, the Lord, shine.

34The water in which You play is the Daughter of the Sun [the Yamuna]; those who have taken shelter of You are the blessed residents of Vraja. Your wish to reach [Vrindavana], Lord, is as empty as a cloud's thirst to find water.

35And this Ganga, O Lord, having come into Vanga, through contact with You purifies the world again. May Your Lordship go from here to Shantipura and purify our house there."10

36Gaura, honouring his words, put on the cloth and crossed the river in that boat with Advaita, Mukunda and Shesha [Nityananda].

37"Ah, My elder, most venerable — the moon of the ocean of Padmavati's womb — has tricked Me and brought Me into Vanga!" — with this thought He entered the town.11

38When the Lord entered Shantipura — happily unseen by those who hold false doctrines — He was surrounded by women with disordered garments and ornaments and by men absorbed in praising Him.

39Some standing near Him said: "This is no man — this is the son of Soma, or the Bodiless One, descended here to sport with Ila and to increase the festival of love of the renunciants."12

40Others, seeing Him possessing nothing, said nothing, only looked at one another; having given Him the treasures of their eyes and hearts, they stood still like statues.

41The best of Acharyas brought the noble One into his house, honoured Him with a seat and so on, and then, together with his wife Sita, began to prepare alms for Him in the house.

42She prepared many dishes — things to chew, suck, drink and lick: rice of six kinds, with ghee, mung, washed — of various tastes, nectarean, clear;

43payasa, barley porridge, sour soup, many vegetable dishes of different sweetness, many cakes — of rice, urad, wheat and barley;

44vadas fried in plenty of cow's ghee, crisp and tasty; dishes with young fruits and pieces of plantain; greens tasting like nectar;

45fruits — seasonal ones, in clusters, young mangoes, bananas, jackfruit and the like; drinks without number, with curd, milk and cream.

46The Acharya, at once filling beautiful cups with these and similar offerings rich in taste, in three portions, offered them to Achyuta, and then, to feed the two brothers with devotion, seated them there, in Hari's house.13

47Seeing this, the younger brother of the avadhuta, though pleased, said to the best of brahmins: "Such abundant alms are not fitting for mendicant monks. It is not good, venerable sir, to leave remnants; so give Me a little of this — something without taste."

[p. 31]

48He, skilled in speech, with joined palms, lovingly answered His true and wholesome words: "According to the Shruti You, Lord, are the one Eater; for such as You such food is fitting — is it not a mere handful?"14

49Hearing the words of Sita's husband, Gaurachandra smiled, began with His elder brother to eat all of it and, seated, jesting, tasting the vegetables and rice, asking "And what is this? And what is this?" — gave him joy.

50Then Nityananda said to Advaita-deva: "I came here to break my fast after fasting five days; looking at your fare now, I think that by ill fate the brahmin must [again] go hungry today."

51Advaita answered him, laughing: "Sir, this is just right for you, a ploughman and a great eater! I know: such a one cannot fill his belly-pot. You, a sannyasi, my lord, are punishing us brahmins."

52Hearing this, the avadhuta, with feigned anger — "Why do you tease a mendicant?" — flung the alms-rice. At that Advaita, at once in ecstasy, danced with tears in his eyes, and the two [brothers], seeing him overflowing with prema, laughed with joy.15

53Having eaten the rice and the rest abundantly and well, having performed achamana with pure water given by Advaita, refreshed [with betel] with camphor, cardamom and tulasi buds, the two, satisfied, anointed with sandal and the like, fell sweetly asleep.

54Advaita, wishing to massage the Lord's lotus feet, at His command first ate with Mukunda and the other devotees; and the Lord, after sleeping a little, rose in the afternoon and held sankirtana with His devotees and the avadhuta.

55So ten days passed. Then the best of Acharyas [Acharyamani], seating Shachi in front in a palanquin, came with the townspeople to that town to see Gaurachandra — and, though worn with hunger, did not rest anywhere for a moment.

56Loudly crying "Hari, Hari!" they reached that [abode] where the lamp of Navadvipa-dhama was staying;16 Advaita quickly lodged them all in the outer quarters, and Shachi, with tears in her eyes, entered Advaita's inner apartments.

[p. 32]

57Seeing that His mother had come, the Lord, after the sankirtana, fell again and again [at her feet] on the ground, scorched by her grief. And she, weeping, long embraced Him, worn as He was — with only the shikha left after His lovely curls were shorn — and said: "My child, is it you?.."

58Clasping her feet and consoling His mother with humble words, Gaura lovingly went out, wishing to see the devotees from the town; and they, seeing Him in saffron garments, with a thin shikha, with only the thread for ornament, fell to the ground with broken hearts.

59Raising them one by one — Vakreshvara and the others, Srivasa, Shridhara, the humble Sri Vidyanidhi, Gangadasa and other brahmins, Buddhimanta Khan and others, all the townspeople down to the cowherds, children and elders — the Lord gladdened them.

60Advaita Prabhu entertained those who had come — gave them fine quarters, food and drink, shrikhanda, seats, beds and so on; and Gaurachandra, worshipping Hari morning and evening with the townspeople — with singing and dancing — and then cherished by His mother, stayed there.17

61In the Sri Gaura-krishnodaya, composed for the delight of connoisseurs by Govinda — a bee intoxicated by tasting the drops of honey that open within the lotus feet of Sri Gauranga, the bull among the lords of sannyasis — the sixth canto, on sannyasa, has come to its close.

Thus ends the sixth canto of the Sri Gaura-krishnodaya composed by Sri Govinda.

Notes

  1. CC Adi 17: the students, irritated because the Lord had beaten one of them with a stick, insulted Him; the Lord thought that unless they were saved they would perish, whereas to a sannyasi they would bow — and so be purified. Therefore He decided to take sannyasa.
  2. CC Adi 17 and Madhya 3 briefly; in more detail the CB, Madhya-khanda. "Those who wear garments of bark" — hermits.
  3. Jagate jagaj-jani-kṛtā tvam asi hy upadīpitā (checked against the scan). The sense of vv. 9–10: the Creator kindled her for the world like a lamp, but her beauty, like lightning, does not last.
  4. Cf. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (2.4.5): "Not for the husband's sake is the husband dear, but for the sake of the Atman." In Govinda-deva this Atman is Hari, "the Enchanting One" (Manohara). The farewell conversation with Vishnupriya — cf. CB, Madhya-khanda; in Murari and Lochana Dasa — in detail.
  5. Nirmālya-puṭīm iva, "like a leaf-cup with nirmalya" (the remnants of a flower offering, which are reverently set aside). The word nibhalye before it is unclear in the edition (checked against the scan).
  6. Chakravakas, according to poetic convention, are separated at night; here it is the reverse: the young spouses were together at night and parted at dawn.
  7. Sannyasa at Katwa — CC Adi 17, Madhya 3. Govinda-deva stresses that the Lord kept the shikha and the thread, and calls the initiation "Vaishnava" (v. 21) — that is, he depicts the Lord's sannyasa as a Vaishnava sannyasa. Cf. 6.57–58: before His mother's eyes is a "thin shikha."
  8. Three days in Radha-desha — CC Madhya 3. "Tapas" is the month of Magha; CC (Adi 17): the Lord took sannyasa at the end of His twenty-fourth year, in the bright fortnight of Magha.
  9. CC Madhya 3: Nityananda told the cowherd boys to show the Lord the way to the Ganga, saying it was the road to Vrindavana; the Lord entered the Ganga, taking it for the Yamuna. The companions' jest: the Ganga flows from the toe of Vishnu's foot.
  10. CC Madhya 3: Advaita met the Lord in a boat, gave Him a dry cloth and said: "Wherever You are, there is Vrindavana," — and the Lord understood that Nityananda had tricked Him.
  11. Padmavati is Nityananda's mother. "Elder": so the Lord respectfully calls Nityananda (cf. 6.47: Gaura is "the avadhuta's younger brother").
  12. The son of Soma (the Moon) is Budha, the husband of Ila. A pun: ilā also means "earth." "Renunciants" — sannyasis.
  13. CC Madhya 3: Sita and Advaita prepared a huge feast for the Lord and Nityananda; Govinda-deva lists the dishes, as does Krishnadasa Kaviraja.
  14. Cf. Brahma-sutra 1.2.9 (attā carācara-grahaṇāt): "The Eater is [the Supreme], for He takes in the moving and the unmoving." Advaita jests: to Him who eats the whole universe this meal is but a handful.
  15. CC Madhya 3: the jesting quarrel of Advaita and Nityananda at the meal and the rice flung by Nityananda — a loving squabble between two friends; Advaita dances on receiving the remnants.
  16. The edition reads prāpur yasmin vayasi sa navadvīpa-dhāma-pradīpaḥ (checked against the scan); vayasi ("at the age") makes no sense here — probably a misprint for vasati, "dwells". We translate the emended text.
  17. CC Madhya 3: Shachi and all the people of Navadvipa came to Shantipura; the Lord spent ten days there in kirtan, and Shachi cooked for Him. Buddhimanta-khāna-mukhyān (v. 59): "headed by Buddhimanta Khan", a devotee of Navadvipa (CC Adi 10).
